 38|
 39|‘도대체 뭐지?’
 40|

 59|“다섯 걸음. 다섯 걸음이라.”

 65|‘성치 않은 저 몸으로 노부를 다섯 걸음이나 물러서게 만들다니.’
 66|

 68|

 70|

 73|‘적이라면 가장 큰 걸림돌이 될 것이나, 아군이 된다면 머지않아 삼성(三星)조차 뛰어넘을 괴물.’
 74|
 75|사로잡더라도 포섭하지 못하리라는 생각은 추호도 하지 않았다.
 76|
 77|그분.
 78|
 79|천주(天主)를 뵙게 된다면, 그 항거할 수 없는 절대자의 힘을 한 번이라도 느끼게 된다면 그분의 앞에 무릎 꿇을 수밖에 없을 테니까.
 80|
 81|과거의 자신이 그러했듯이.
 82|
 83|“천주께 데려가야겠군. 반드시.”
 84|
 85|창공이 그렇게 뇌까린 바로 그 순간이었다.
 86|
 87|“누구를, 누구한테 데려간다고?”
 88|
 89|스아아아.
 90|
 91|건조한 목소리와 함께 반경 수십여 장의 공기가 뜨겁게 달아오른다.

 93|지면 위에서 피어오르는 아지랑이 너머로 다가오는 민머리의 중년인을 확인한 창공이 창백한 입술을 달싹였다.
 94|
 95|“화왕(火王) 적천강.”
 96|
 97|“노부의 존함을 어딜 함부로 입에 올리느냐, 이 불알 없는 놈아.”
 98|
 99|“누가 사제지간 아니랄까 봐 언행이 쏙 빼닮았군. 제자가 스승에게 배운 것인지, 스승이 제자에게 배운 것인지는 모르겠지만.”
100|
101|적천강이 시큰둥하게 대답했다.
102|
103|“보통은 제자가 스승에게 배우는 법이니라. 네놈처럼 뿌리도 없는 호로새끼는 모르겠지만.”
104|
105|“뿌리라, 한때는 내게도 그런 것이 있었지. 가족과도 같았던 스승과 사형제들도.”
106|
107|“그렇군. 그럼 멀쩡한 불알을 자르는 것도 네놈 스승에게 배운 게냐?”
108|
109|“아니.”
110|
111|창공의 입가에 살기 어린 미소가 번졌다.
112|
113|“그 어떤 상황에서도 스스로의 뿌리를 잊지 말라는 가르침을 받았지. 그런 스승님의 말씀을, 나는 단 한 순간도 잊어 본 적이 없다.”
114|
115|“네놈에게 무슨 구구절절한 사연이 있는지는 모르겠지만…… 가르침이고 나발이고 더는 기억하지 않아도 될 게다.”
116|
117|적천강이 주먹을 들어 올리며 씩 웃었다.
118|
119|“이거 한 방 맞은 놈들은 전부 그렇게 됐으니.”
120|
121|그리고 주위를 힐끗 둘러보며 덧붙였다.
122|
123|“뭐, 굳이 노부가 아니어도 네놈을 찢어 죽이고 싶어 하는 것들은 널리고 널린 것 같지만.”
124|
125|적천강의 말은 결코 과장이 아니었다.
126|
127|무려 이천에 달하는 금의위.
128|
129|하나같이 초일류에서 절정의 무위를 지닌 대국 제일의 정예군이 그들을 둥그렇게 에워싸고 있었으니까.
130|
131|그뿐인가.
132|
133|황제와 황실을 수호하는 금의위보다는 한 수 떨어진다는 평가를 받지만, 역시 정예라고 부르기에는 손색이 없는 금위군들까지 뒤늦게 합류하여 대연회장의 외벽을 점령하여 활시위를 겨누고 있었다.
134|
135|물경 오천에 달하는 머릿수.
136|
137|일군(一軍)이라 칭하기에 일말의 부족함도 없을뿐더러, 그 병력의 질은 가히 십만 대군과도 비견될 정도.
138|
139|그러나 창공은 담담하게 사방을 둘러싼 무수한 창칼과 화살촉을 바라볼 뿐이었다.
140|
141|정확히는 그들의 어깨너머, 높게 솟은 단 위에서 자신을 바라보고 있는 한 사람을.
142|
143|“목줄 풀린 사냥개들은 죽을 자리도 못 알아보고 날뛰는데, 약아빠진 주인은 뒷전에 앉아 구경만 하는군.”
144|
145|언제나 그랬듯이.
146|
147|작게 덧붙인 창공이 소리 내어 웃었다.
148|
149|그리고 불현듯.
150|
151|뚝. 하고 끊어진 웃음소리와 함께 그의 창백한 입술 사이로 거대한 외침이 터져 나왔다.
152|
153|“쳐라-!”
154|
155|콰아아아!
156|
157|음성에 실린 미증유의 공력이 대연회장을 뒤흔든 그 순간.
158|
159|푹! 서걱!
160|
161|금의위 중 하나의 가슴 위로 눈부신 검신이 솟아올랐다. 고통도 잊은 채, 황금빛 갑옷을 관통한 그것을 멍하니 바라보던 그가 더듬거리는 목소리로 중얼거렸다.
162|
163|“도, 도대체 왜…….”
164|
165|부릅떠진 눈동자에 서린 것은 경악인 동시에 불신이었다.
166|
167|빠르게 죽음이 다가오는 와중에도, 그는 진심으로 알고 싶었다.
168|
169|왜, 어찌하여 이토록 어이없게 죽음을 맞이해야 하는 것인지.
170|
171|십 년이 넘도록 호형호제했던 동기가 왜 뒤에서 자신을 찔렀는지.
172|
173|“크륵. 도, 동 형?”
174|
175|왜일까.
176|
177|어째서일까.
178|
179|비록 피를 나누지는 않았으나 의형제로 여기겠다고 했다.
180|
181|함께 격려하고 의를 다지며 이 나라와 황제 폐하께 충성을 다하자고 수십, 수백 번도 넘게 술잔을 기울이며 이야기했다.
182|
183|그러나 끓어오르는 핏물을 참으며 토해 낸 그 외마디 부름에 돌아온 대답은, 지난 십 년간 들어 본 적 없는 무미건조한 목소리였다.
184|
185|“천상천하(天上天下). 만마앙복(萬魔仰伏).”
186|
187|“……!”
188|
189|그것이 마지막이었다.
190|
191|콰득.
192|
193|비틀어 내며 뽑히는 검신과 함께 혼이 떠난 육신이 나동그라진다.
194|
195|곳곳에서.
196|
197|푹!
198|
199|온 사방에서.
200|
201|서걱!
202|
203|수도 없이.
204|
205|촤아아악!
206|
207|깔끔하게 베어진 목이 지면으로 굴러떨어지고, 잘려 나간 사지와 핏물이 허공으로 솟구쳤다.
208|
209|이천에 달했던 금의위 중, 물경 수백의 목숨이 그렇게 찰나지간에 사라졌다.
210|
211|상관. 수하. 혹은 형제처럼 아꼈던 자신들의 동료에 의해서.
212|
213|“……!”
214|
215|“……!”
216|
217|사방에서 먹먹한 고함이 터져 나왔다. 배반한 자와 배반당한 자. 지키려는 자와 빼앗으려는 자가 서로를 향해 얽혀들었다.
218|
219|카카카캉!
220|
221|서걱! 푹!
222|
223|끄아아아악!
224|
225|메아리와도 같은 비명과 함께 어둠 속에서 번갯불과도 같은 검광(劍光)이 쉴 새 없이 번뜩인다.
226|
227|횃불을 들고 있던 누군가의 손이 피 웅덩이에 잠겨 꿈틀거렸다.
228|
229|그리고 어둠 속에서 순식간에 벌어진 이 끔찍한 난전(亂戰) 위로, 또 다른 어둠이 덧씌워졌다.
230|
231|솨아아아아.
232|
233|그 소리를 들은 누군가는 비가 내린다고 생각했고, 죽음을 기다리며 헐떡이던 또 다른 누군가는 그리움 속 고향의 드넓은 평원을 떠올렸다.
234|
235|저 멀리서 불어온 세찬 바람이 평원을 휩쓸면 꼭 이런 소리가 났었으니까.
236|
237|잘 익은 곡식과 풀이 허리를 굽히고, 마을 잔치가 벌어졌던 커다란 거목(巨木)은 풍성한 가지와 잎사귀를 흔들었으니까.
238|
239|하지만 두 번 다시 그리운 고향으로 돌아가지 못하리라는 것을, 이름 모를 그는 깨달았다.
240|
241|‘아.’
242|
243|하늘 위로 덧씌워진 어둠이, 아니 헤아릴 수 없이 무수한 화살의 비가 쏟아져 내리고 있었다.
244|
245|그들의 머리 위로, 혹은 그들이 충성을 바치는 황제를 향해서 공간을 뒤덮으며 나아가고 있었다.
246|
247|쿨럭.
248|
249|내장 조각이 섞인 핏물을 내뱉으며 그는 마음속으로 중얼거렸다.
250|
251|이건 아니었는데.
252|
253|내가 고향을, 가족을 떠난 이유는 이렇게 허무하기 죽기 위해서가 아니었는데.
254|
255|‘빌어먹을.’
256|
257|그는 멍하니 짓쳐 드는 어둠을 바라보았다. 이 끔찍한 통증과 절망을 끝내줄 죽음을 기다렸다.
258|
259|그리고 보았다.
260|
261|화륵, 콰아아아!
262|
263|어둠을 집어삼키는 거대한 화염을.
264|
265|무수한 화살들을 형체도 남기지 않고 불태우는 그 압도적인 열기 속에서, 먹이를 낚아채는 한 마리의 매처럼 지상으로 낙하하는 한 청년을.
266|
267|콰앙!
268|
269|분명 천둥 같아야 할 굉음이, 수백여 장은 떨어져 있는 것처럼 흐릿하게 들리는 것은 왜일까.
270|
271|그는 어두워지는 시야 속에서 생각했다.
272|
273|저 청년의 이름이 무엇이었는지.
274|
275|살려 달라는 그 한 마디가, 고향으로 돌려보내 달라는 그 짧은 부탁이 왜 목소리가 되어 흘러나오지 못하는지.
276|
277|눈앞에 드리워지는 어둠 속에서, 그는 다만 지켜볼 수밖에 없었다.
278|
279|쉴 새 없이 쏟아지는 화살 비를 불태우는 화염과 청년이 움직일 때마다 짚단처럼 쓰러져 가는 배신자들을.
280|
281|자신과 같은 피륙으로 이루어진 인간이라고는 믿을 수 없는, 경천동지(驚天動地)의 전투를 시작한 두 존재를.
282|
283|쾅! 쾅! 콰아아앙!
284|
285|뜨거운 열기가. 몸서리치는 한기가.
286|
287|쉬지 않고 사방을 물들이는 화염과 새하얀 섬광이 밤을 불태우고 얼어 붙인다.
288|

Cang Gong saw a bald, middle-aged man approaching through the heat haze rising from the ground. His pale lips parted.

[P44]
“Fire King Jeok Cheongang.”

[P45]
“How dare you toss this old man’s name around, you ball-less bastard?”

[P46]
“You two really are alike in speech and behavior. I can’t tell whether the disciple learned from the master or the master from the disciple.”

[P47]
Jeok Cheongang answered flatly. “Usually, the disciple learns from the master. Though a rootless bastard like you wouldn’t know that.”

[P48]
“Roots, huh? I had those once. A master and fellow disciples who were like family.”

[P49]
“I see. So did your master teach you to cut off your own balls, too?”

[P50]
“No.”

[P51]
A murderous smile spread across Cang Gong’s lips.

[P52]
“He taught me never to forget my roots, no matter what happened. I haven’t forgotten his words for a single moment.”

[P53]
“I don’t know what long-winded story you’ve got, but to hell with his teachings. You won’t need to remember them anymore.”

[P54]
Jeok Cheongang raised his fist and grinned.

[P55]
“Everyone who’s taken a hit from this old man ended up that way.”

[P56]
He glanced around and added, “Though it looks like plenty of others would love to tear you apart, too.”

[P57]
He wasn’t exaggerating.

[P58]
Nearly two thousand members of the Embroidered Uniform Guard surrounded them. Every one of them belonged to the Great Nation’s finest force, with martial arts ranging from Supreme First Rate to Peak.

[P59]
And that wasn’t all.

[P60]
The Imperial Guards were considered a cut below the Embroidered Uniform Guard, who protected the Emperor and the imperial family, but they were elite troops in their own right. They’d arrived late, taken positions on the outer walls of the Grand Banquet Hall, and drawn their bows.

[P61]
Five thousand men in all.

[P62]
More than enough to call an army—and in quality, they could rival a force of a hundred thousand.

[P63]
Yet Cang Gong merely looked at the countless spears, swords, and arrowheads surrounding him.

[P64]
Or rather, he looked past them to the one man watching him from the high platform.

[P65]
“The hunting dogs have slipped their leashes and are running wild, too stupid to know where they’ll die. Meanwhile, their cunning master sits back and watches.”

[P66]
*Just as he always has.*

[P67]
Cang Gong laughed aloud.

[P68]
Then his laughter stopped dead, and a thunderous command burst from his pale lips.

[P69]
“Attack!”

[P70]
*BOOOOM!*

[P71]
The immense internal energy carried in his voice shook the Grand Banquet Hall. At that instant—

[P72]
*Thrust! Slash!*

[P73]
A gleaming sword blade burst from an Embroidered Uniform Guard’s chest. Too stunned even to feel the pain, he stared at the steel piercing his golden armor.

[P74]
“W-Why…?”

[P75]
Shock and disbelief filled his wide eyes.

[P76]
Even as death rushed toward him, he wanted to know.

[P77]
Why was he dying like this? Why had a comrade he’d called hyung for more than ten years stabbed him in the back?

[P78]
“Ghk. D-Dong hyung?”

[P79]
Why?

[P80]
They weren’t related by blood, but they’d promised to treat each other as sworn brothers.

[P81]
Dozens—hundreds—of times, they’d raised their cups together, encouraging each other, pledging their brotherhood and swearing loyalty to their country and His Majesty the Emperor.

[P82]
But when he forced out that one call through the blood rising in his throat, the answer came in a flat voice he’d never heard in all their ten years together.

[P83]
“Heaven above, earth below. All demons bow in reverence.”

[P84]
“…!”

[P85]
Those were the last words he heard.

[P86]
*Crunch.*

[P87]
The sword twisted and pulled free. His lifeless body toppled to the ground.

[P88]
Elsewhere—

[P89]
*Thrust!*

[P90]
All around—

[P91]
*Slash!*

[P92]
Again and again—

[P93]
*Shhhk!*

[P94]
Severed heads rolled across the ground. Limbs and blood flew through the air.

[P95]
In the blink of an eye, hundreds of the two thousand Embroidered Uniform Guards were dead.

[P96]
Killed by their own comrades. By superiors, subordinates, and men they’d cherished like brothers.

[P97]
“…!”

[P98]
“…!”

[P99]
Strangled shouts rose on every side. The traitors and the betrayed, those fighting to protect and those fighting to take, clashed.

[P100]
*Clang-clang-clang!*

[P101]
*Slash! Thrust!*

[P102]
“Aaagh!”

[P103]
Screams echoed as swordlight flashed ceaselessly through the darkness.

[P104]
Someone’s hand, still clutching a torch, twitched in a pool of blood.

[P105]
Then another darkness spread over the horrific melee that had erupted beneath the night sky.

[P106]
*Fwoooooosh.*

[P107]
Some who heard the sound thought it was rain. Another man, panting as he waited for death, remembered the broad plains of his hometown.

[P108]
A strong wind sweeping in from far away had made just such a sound across those fields.

[P109]
The ripe grain and grasses would bow, and the great tree where the village held its festivals would shake its abundant branches and leaves.

[P110]
But the nameless man knew he would never see his hometown again.

[P111]
*Ah.*

[P112]
The darkness spreading across the sky was no darkness at all. Countless arrows were raining down.

[P113]
They filled the air as they flew toward the men below—or toward the Emperor those men had sworn to serve.

[P114]
*Cough.*

[P115]
He spat blood mixed with fragments of his innards.

[P116]
*This wasn’t how it was supposed to be.*

[P117]
He hadn’t left his family and his hometown to die so pointlessly.

[P118]
*Damn it.*

[P119]
He stared at the darkness rushing toward him and waited for death to end his pain and despair.

[P120]
Then he saw it.

[P121]
*Fwoosh—BOOOOM!*

[P122]
A great blaze swallowed the darkness.

[P123]
Countless arrows burned away without a trace. Through that overwhelming heat, a young man plunged toward the ground like a hawk diving for prey.

[P124]
*BOOM!*

[P125]
Why did a roar that should have sounded like thunder reach him so faintly, as though it had come from hundreds of yards away?

[P126]
As his vision dimmed, he tried to remember the young man’s name.

[P127]
Why couldn’t he say it? Why couldn’t he ask him to save him, to send him home?

[P128]
With darkness closing over his eyes, all he could do was watch. Flames consumed the unending rain of arrows, and traitors fell like bundles of straw wherever the young man moved.

[P129]
Two beings began a battle that shook heaven and earth. He could hardly believe they were made of flesh and blood like him.

[P130]
*Bang! Bang! BOOOOM!*

[P131]
Scorching heat. Shuddering cold.

[P132]
Flames and white flashes swept the hall without pause, setting the night ablaze and freezing it over.

[P133]
The countless bodies still piling up amid sprays of blood served as firewood.

[P134]
And the life of one unfortunate man, made to suffer a little longer than the rest, as a sacrifice.

[P135]
At the end of that terrible wait, the nameless Embroidered Uniform Guard remembered the young man’s name.

[P136]
*Jin Taekyung. Right. It was Jin Taekyung.*

[P137]
Strange.

[P138]
He lay dying in a pool of blood, in the middle of a sea of corpses and blood, yet he didn’t feel cold at all.

[P139]
*It’s warm.*

[P140]
He watched the flames surging between flashing spears and swords. Then, unable to fight the sleep overtaking him, he closed his eyes.

[P141]
He thought of the hometown he would never return to.

[P142]
* * *

[P143]
People who love to talk say only two things can kill a Supreme Peak master: time and his own carelessness.

[P144]
Right now, I wanted to tell those people one thing.

[P145]
*Then why don’t you try fighting them?*

[P146]
A Supreme Peak master is still made of flesh and blood.

[P147]
To someone who doesn’t know any better, he might look like a superhuman who can take down hundreds or thousands of enemies. But he has limits.

[P148]
Especially when at least half those enemies are Peak masters.

[P149]
*Swish! Slice!*

[P150]
A thrust spearhead skimmed my cheek. The internal energy behind it sliced my skin anyway—that came standard. The punch I gave its owner was a bonus.

[P151]
*Wham!*

[P152]
My Flame Divine Palm struck the Embroidered Uniform Guard—no, the traitor planted by Dark Heaven—in the chest. He flew backward like a puppet with its strings cut.

[P153]
Dead on the spot.

[P154]
But someone else filled the gap. The others moved more cautiously now, and faster.

[P155]
*Damn it.*

[P156]
If they’d only been martial artists, they would’ve been much easier to deal with. But they were soldiers, too—a force with both powerful martial arts and an army’s discipline.

[P157]
*Slash! Thrust!*

[P158]
I snatched a spear from someone’s hands and swung it at every enemy in reach, glaring past their shoulders.

[P159]
*Why the hell?!*

[P160]
I wanted to shout it.

[P161]
Why weren’t they helping? How could they stand there and watch, even now?

[P162]
The Emperor stood where I was looking. Baek Yeon and So Gyo remained beside him, guarding him like stone statues.

[P163]
And now there was someone else in my line of sight.

[P164]
An unwelcome guest.

[P165]
*Whoosh!*

[P166]
A sharp sound cut through the air. A dozen or so Embroidered Uniform Guards who’d been fighting nearby stopped moving.

[P167]
Their eyes widened in disbelief.

[P168]
Faint lines appeared across their necks, darkening by the second.

[P169]
*Gurgle—SHHHK!*

[P170]
Blood beaded along the cuts, then sprayed like fountains. The man who’d swept past them watched their bodies fall like rotten trees. He looked at me and sighed.

[P171]
“Why did you do it? If you’d simply trusted me and followed along, everything could have gone smoothly.”

[P172]
Instead of answering Ma Sanbao’s bullshit—so obvious even the mutt next door could understand it—I brought my spearhead down.

[P173]
*Whoosh!*

[P174]
[^1]: A Hongmen Banquet is a treacherous feast, named for a historical banquet at which an assassination was attempted.

# Mastering Adjudicator Brief

You are a **veto**, not a second novelist and not a gloss writer.

This call is isolated, non-interactive, and tool-free. The packet already contains the Korean source, both complete English versions, glossary matches, rules, and every numbered hunk. Do not call tools, search the repository, or read files. Do not announce a plan.

The first editor (SOL) has already rewritten the accepted English (BASELINE) for fluency. Default is `SOL`. Take `BASE` only when SOL is actually unfaithful. Write `REPAIR` only when **both** BASE and SOL are unfaithful.

## Default

Choose `SOL` unless a veto below fires.

Keep SOL when it is slangier, punchier, more spoken, or more idiomatic and the Korean sense holds (`기만질` → “con me”, `톡톡히` → “full Peak Master treatment”, `득실거리다` → “crawling with”, `인간 백정` → “butcher of men”, `한 몸` → “are one”, `시원하다` in a bath → “That’s the stuff”, `어렵게 찾아오고 쉽게 깨지는 법` → “hard-won and easily broken”). If SOL already naturalized Korean syntax (`이 혁무진` → “I, Hyuk Mujin”), keep SOL. Do not reproduce Korean word order.

**Literal closeness to Korean wording is not fidelity.** Preserve the source’s meaning and effect in natural English.

## Veto — choose `BASE`

Use `BASE` only for a real miss:

* wrong denotation, quantity, hedge, category, subject/object, or physical action
* a different English idiom than the Korean joke (`까발리다` ≠ “gives someone away”; `넉살` ≠ “banter”)
* a rebuilt joke whose comic machine BASE already has (`얼마나 …는지 …겠다` must stay a simple exaggeration: “snored so loudly even my mother in Ilsan probably heard him,” not “You had to wonder how loudly…”)
* dropped image, attitude, or timing
* SOL replaces an established project rendering, System label, or Markdown convention with an unsupported synonym
* SOL stamps `hyung` (or another kinship title) onto every narrative name when BASE already uses the name and the Korean `형` is ordinary reference, not a vocative or a topical joke (`진호 형` → Jinho in narration)

Do not veto SOL for being informal. Do not veto SOL to “clarify” slang. Do not veto SOL merely because BASELINE is already understandable.

## `REPAIR` only when both fail

Example: `겹경사가 따로 없다` means two good things **together** (double blessing). `따로` is not “separate.” If BASE says “entirely separate stroke of luck” and SOL says “unexpected windfall,” `REPAIR` to stacked luck.

## Critical binding translation rules

# Translation Rules

## Fidelity

- Translate the Korean source—not the wiki, manhwa, fan translations, or expected plot.
- Semantic fidelity outranks elegance. Never improve rhythm, humor, or localization by changing a physical action, negation, relationship, hierarchy, mechanism, quantity, or causal detail.
- Preserve every fact, causal link, joke, emotional beat, repetition, and intentional omission. Add nothing.
- Preserve small action verbs and pragmatic cues exactly: nodding versus shaking one's head, pretending nothing happened, and mild or approachable impressions are characterization, not expendable texture.
- Preserve viewpoint and tense. Resolve omitted subjects only when context supports it; retain genuine ambiguity.
- Match each speaker's hierarchy, intimacy, humor, and profanity naturally. Do not mechanically retain every honorific or classical self-reference.
- Do not censor or soften content.

## Terminology

- `compendium.md` and `docs/NAMES.md` are binding for established names, titles, ranks, techniques, organizations, system terms, items, and locations. Profile headings and aliases join that ledger.
- Search only exact Korean terms already present in the current chapter; the compendium contains future-sensitive entries.
- Never re-romanize established names or invent grand names for uncertain terms. First use of an unlisted name or title almost always needs a footnote or a mapped ledger term.
- Use `qi` for Murim energy and `mana` for the modern Hunter system when the source distinguishes them. Preserve an established chapter-specific rendering such as `internal energy` when the exact glossary and surrounding Korean distinguish accumulated `공력` from resulting `기운`.
- In System panels, render `등급` as `**Grade:**` for quest, item, skill, and martial-art classifications. Reserve `rank` for Hunter classifications or ordinary prose; never replace a System `Grade` field with `Rank`.

## English and Markdown

- Use contemporary US English and natural action-comedy prose; avoid Korean syntax calques and generic cultivation MTL phrasing.
- File: `translations/NNNN.md`; heading: `# Chapter N`.
- Speech: curly double quotes. Direct thoughts: italics without quotes.
- Use em dashes without spaces, the ellipsis character `…`, and `* * *` for source scene breaks.
- Format each actual game System-message panel as one Markdown blockquote window headed `> **System**`. Keep all consecutive notices, fields, and lines inside that same blockquote; separate windows when prose intervenes. Do not enclose System notices or UI terms in square brackets; the `System` heading and framed blockquote identify the panel. Do not label manuals, ordinary quotations, warnings printed in a manual, or other non-System material as `System`; use a normal blockquote or a specific heading instead. Do not wrap each complete notice in outer `**`; retain bold only for meaningful labels or emphasis inside the panel.
- Keep the final file English-only reading copy: no audit notes, Korean text, summaries, or model metadata.

### Tone and Style

- Write like a polished commercial webnovel: brisk, vivid, accessible, and easy to read aloud.
- Preserve the series’ contrast between danger and comedy. Let absurdity, bad timing, blunt reactions, and grim situations create dark humor without adding jokes absent from the Korean.
- Jin Taekyung’s narration is conversational, observant, self-mocking, and occasionally profane. It may be irreverent even when the situation is serious.
- Keep deadpan punchlines short and well-timed. Do not explain a joke after delivering it.
- Preserve the source's level of explicitness. A euphemism may remain euphemistic even when its meaning is sexual or crude; do not replace it with more graphic English merely for impact.
- Make dialogue spontaneous and character-specific. Preserve hierarchy and intimacy through word choice, address, rhythm, and restraint—not archaic wuxia English.
- Use strong profanity when the Korean is strong, but neither intensify nor sanitize it. Do not make ordinary lines uniformly vulgar. Profanity should reveal mood or relationship.
- Keep action and injury vivid but clear rather than purple. Do not make violence funny unless the source’s framing does.
- Avoid stiff literalism, translator-added melodrama, dated internet slang, and quippy superhero-style banter.
- On the second pass, correct awkward English collocations and word choices without changing meaning or voice. Prefer ordinary, spoken English over stiff Latinate or ceremonial wording when the scene is brisk or comic: “goose bumps” rather than “gooseflesh,” and “laid into them” rather than “launched into a solemn denunciation.” Read the prose aloud and replace any phrase that sounds like a formal essay, legal document, or literal dictionary gloss unless the source deliberately calls for that register.

## Footnotes

Use `[^1]` Markdown footnotes when a brief, factual, spoiler-free explanation materially helps an English reader understand:

- a Korean institution, living arrangement, food, holiday, myth, historical reference, or local custom;
- a Korean word, phrase, idiom, wordplay, or culturally specific image that cannot be conveyed fully by the best natural English analogy;
- a deliberately literal rendering whose cultural or linguistic force would otherwise be lost.

For example, render `고시원` as “goshiwon” when the setting or connotations matter, with a concise footnote explaining that it is a very small, inexpensive room-for-rent housing arrangement. Prefer the best natural English analogy in the prose. Use a literal translation plus a concise footnote when the Korean wording itself matters. Define a term at its first meaningful occurrence and do not repeat the note unnecessarily. Footnotes must be rare, useful, and non-spoiling; do not footnote ordinary vocabulary, fully preserved jokes, or uncertainty. Record consequential uncertainty in `docs/STATE.md`.

## Spoilers and Scope

- Safe profiles contain only facts revealed through the latest completed chapter.
- Never read `characters/spoilers/` during drafting. Reviewers may consult one relevant sealed profile only for a specific unresolved continuity issue after the draft is complete.
- Future knowledge may prevent contradiction but may not add early names, pronouns, certainty, motives, or foreshadowing.
- Translate exactly one requested chapter unless the user explicitly requests a batch. Never modify Korean source files under `source/`.

- In System panels, render `등급` as `**Grade:**` for quest, item, skill, and martial-art classifications. Reserve `rank` for Hunter classifications or ordinary prose; never replace a System `Grade` field with `Rank`.

## English and Markdown

- Use contemporary US English and natural action-comedy prose; avoid Korean syntax calques and generic cultivation MTL phrasing.
- File: `translations/NNNN.md`; heading: `# Chapter N`.
- Speech: curly double quotes. Direct thoughts: italics without quotes.
- Use em dashes without spaces, the ellipsis character `…`, and `* * *` for source scene breaks.
- Format each actual game System-message panel as one Markdown blockquote window headed `> **System**`. Keep all consecutive notices, fields, and lines inside that same blockquote; separate windows when prose intervenes. Do not enclose System notices or UI terms in square brackets; the `System` heading and framed blockquote identify the panel. Do not label manuals, ordinary quotations, warnings printed in a manual, or other non-System material as `System`; use a normal blockquote or a specific heading instead. Do not wrap each complete notice in outer `**`; retain bold only for meaningful labels or emphasis inside the panel.
- Keep the final file English-only reading copy: no audit notes, Korean text, summaries, or model metadata.

### Tone and Style

- Write like a polished commercial webnovel: brisk, vivid, accessible, and easy to read aloud.
- Preserve the series’ contrast between danger and comedy. Let absurdity, bad timing, blunt reactions, and grim situations create dark humor without adding jokes absent from the Korean.
- Jin Taekyung’s narration is conversational, observant, self-mocking, and occasionally profane. It may be irreverent even when the situation is serious.
- Keep deadpan punchlines short and well-timed. Do not explain a joke after delivering it.
- Preserve the source's level of explicitness. A euphemism may remain euphemistic even when its meaning is sexual or crude; do not replace it with more graphic English merely for impact.
- Make dialogue spontaneous and character-specific. Preserve hierarchy and intimacy through word choice, address, rhythm, and restraint—not archaic wuxia English.
- Use strong profanity when the Korean is strong, but neither intensify nor sanitize it. Do not make ordinary lines uniformly vulgar. Profanity should reveal mood or relationship.
- Keep action and injury vivid but clear rather than purple. Do not make violence funny unless the source’s framing does.
- Avoid stiff literalism, translator-added melodrama, dated internet slang, and quippy superhero-style banter.
- On the second pass, correct awkward English collocations and word choices without changing meaning or voice. Prefer ordinary, spoken English over stiff Latinate or ceremonial wording when the scene is brisk or comic: “goose bumps” rather than “gooseflesh,” and “laid into them” rather than “launched into a solemn denunciation.” Read the prose aloud and replace any phrase that sounds like a formal essay, legal document, or literal dictionary gloss unless the source deliberately calls for that register.

## Footnotes

Use `[^1]` Markdown footnotes when a brief, factual, spoiler-free explanation materially helps an English reader understand:

- a Korean institution, living arrangement, food, holiday, myth, historical reference, or local custom;
- a Korean word, phrase, idiom, wordplay, or culturally specific image that cannot be conveyed fully by the best natural English analogy;
- a deliberately literal rendering whose cultural or linguistic force would otherwise be lost.

For example, render `고시원` as “goshiwon” when the setting or connotations matter, with a concise footnote explaining that it is a very small, inexpensive room-for-rent housing arrangement. Prefer the best natural English analogy in the prose. Use a literal translation plus a concise footnote when the Korean wording itself matters. Define a term at its first meaningful occurrence and do not repeat the note unnecessarily. Footnotes must be rare, useful, and non-spoiling; do not footnote ordinary vocabulary, fully preserved jokes, or uncertainty. Record consequential uncertainty in `docs/STATE.md`.

## Spoilers and Scope

- Safe profiles contain only facts revealed through the latest completed chapter.
- Never read `characters/spoilers/` during drafting. Reviewers may consult one relevant sealed profile only for a specific unresolved continuity issue after the draft is complete.
- Future knowledge may prevent contradiction but may not add early names, pronouns, certainty, motives, or foreshadowing.
- Translate exactly one requested chapter unless the user explicitly requests a batch. Never modify Korean source files under `source/`.

“…!”

*Crunch.*

Elsewhere—

*Thrust!*

All around—

*Slash!*

Again and again—

*Shhhk!*

[P97]
“…!”

[P98]
“…!”

*Clang-clang-clang!*

[P101]
*Slash! Thrust!*

“Aaagh!”

*Fwoooooosh.*

*Ah.*

*Cough.*

*This wasn’t how it was supposed to be.*

*Damn it.*

*Fwoosh—BOOOOM!*

[P124]
*BOOM!*

[P127]

[P130]
*Bang! Bang! BOOOOM!*

*Jin Taekyung. Right. It was Jin Taekyung.*

Strange.

[P138]

[P139]
*It’s warm.*

[P142]
* * *

[P144]
Right now, I wanted to tell those people one thing.

[P145]
*Then why don’t you try fighting them?*

A Supreme Peak master is still made of flesh and blood.

[P147]

*Swish! Slice!*

[P151]
*Wham!*

[P152]

Dead on the spot.

[P154]

[P155]
*Damn it.*

[P156]
If they’d only been martial artists, they would’ve been much easier to deal with. But they were soldiers, too—a force with both powerful martial arts and an army’s discipline.

[P157]
*Slash! Thrust!*

[P158]
I snatched a spear from someone’s hands and swung it at every enemy in reach, glaring past their shoulders.

[P159]
*Why the hell?!*

[P160]
I wanted to shout it.

[P161]
Why weren’t they helping? How could they stand there and watch, even now?

[P162]

[P163]

An unwelcome guest.

[P165]
*Whoosh!*

Their eyes widened in disbelief.

[P169]
*Gurgle—SHHHK!*

[P172]

*Whoosh!*

## Adjudicator rules

# Mastering Adjudicator Brief

You are a **veto**, not a second novelist and not a gloss writer.

This call is isolated, non-interactive, and tool-free. The packet already contains the Korean source, both complete English versions, glossary matches, rules, and every numbered hunk. Do not call tools, search the repository, or read files. Do not announce a plan.

The first editor (SOL) has already rewritten the accepted English (BASELINE) for fluency. Default is `SOL`. Take `BASE` only when SOL is actually unfaithful. Write `REPAIR` only when **both** BASE and SOL are unfaithful.

## Default

Choose `SOL` unless a veto below fires.

Keep SOL when it is slangier, punchier, more spoken, or more idiomatic and the Korean sense holds (`기만질` → “con me”, `톡톡히` → “full Peak Master treatment”, `득실거리다` → “crawling with”, `인간 백정` → “butcher of men”, `한 몸` → “are one”, `시원하다` in a bath → “That’s the stuff”, `어렵게 찾아오고 쉽게 깨지는 법` → “hard-won and easily broken”). If SOL already naturalized Korean syntax (`이 혁무진` → “I, Hyuk Mujin”), keep SOL. Do not reproduce Korean word order.

**Literal closeness to Korean wording is not fidelity.** Preserve the source’s meaning and effect in natural English.

## Veto — choose `BASE`

Use `BASE` only for a real miss:

* wrong denotation, quantity, hedge, category, subject/object, or physical action
* a different English idiom than the Korean joke (`까발리다` ≠ “gives someone away”; `넉살` ≠ “banter”)
* a rebuilt joke whose comic machine BASE already has (`얼마나 …는지 …겠다` must stay a simple exaggeration: “snored so loudly even my mother in Ilsan probably heard him,” not “You had to wonder how loudly…”)
* dropped image, attitude, or timing
* SOL replaces an established project rendering, System label, or Markdown convention with an unsupported synonym
* SOL stamps `hyung` (or another kinship title) onto every narrative name when BASE already uses the name and the Korean `형` is ordinary reference, not a vocative or a topical joke (`진호 형` → Jinho in narration)

Do not veto SOL for being informal. Do not veto SOL to “clarify” slang. Do not veto SOL merely because BASELINE is already understandable.

## `REPAIR` only when both fail

Example: `겹경사가 따로 없다` means two good things **together** (double blessing). `따로` is not “separate.” If BASE says “entirely separate stroke of luck” and SOL says “unexpected windfall,” `REPAIR` to stacked luck.

Do not `REPAIR` a working SOL line. Do not invent a third style because you prefer it.

For `REPAIR`, write the smallest complete replacement needed for that hunk. It must be natural English and fully source-faithful.

## Glossary

Korean **keys** are binding unless the source uses that string in a different ordinary-language sense. Glossary **English** is not a license for a calque (`presiding chair`). If SOL is a natural recast of the same sense, keep SOL.

Return exactly one JSON object and no Markdown fence or prose:

## Critical binding translation rules

# Translation Rules

## Fidelity

- Translate the Korean source—not the wiki, manhwa, fan translations, or expected plot.
- Semantic fidelity outranks elegance. Never improve rhythm, humor, or localization by changing a physical action, negation, relationship, hierarchy, mechanism, quantity, or causal detail.
- Preserve every fact, causal link, joke, emotional beat, repetition, and intentional omission. Add nothing.
- Preserve small action verbs and pragmatic cues exactly: nodding versus shaking one's head, pretending nothing happened, and mild or approachable impressions are characterization, not expendable texture.
- Preserve viewpoint and tense. Resolve omitted subjects only when context supports it; retain genuine ambiguity.
- Match each speaker's hierarchy, intimacy, humor, and profanity naturally. Do not mechanically retain every honorific or classical self-reference.
- Do not censor or soften content.

## Terminology

- `compendium.md` and `docs/NAMES.md` are binding for established names, titles, ranks, techniques, organizations, system terms, items, and locations. Profile headings and aliases join that ledger.
- Search only exact Korean terms already present in the current chapter; the compendium contains future-sensitive entries.
- Never re-romanize established names or invent grand names for uncertain terms. First use of an unlisted name or title almost always needs a footnote or a mapped ledger term.
- Use `qi` for Murim energy and `mana` for the modern Hunter system when the source distinguishes them. Preserve an established chapter-specific rendering such as `internal energy` when the exact glossary and surrounding Korean distinguish accumulated `공력` from resulting `기운`.
- In System panels, render `등급` as `**Grade:**` for quest, item, skill, and martial-art classifications. Reserve `rank` for Hunter classifications or ordinary prose; never replace a System `Grade` field with `Rank`.

## English and Markdown

- Use contemporary US English and natural action-comedy prose; avoid Korean syntax calques and generic cultivation MTL phrasing.
- File: `translations/NNNN.md`; heading: `# Chapter N`.
- Speech: curly double quotes. Direct thoughts: italics without quotes.
- Use em dashes without spaces, the ellipsis character `…`, and `* * *` for source scene breaks.
- Format each actual game System-message panel as one Markdown blockquote window headed `> **System**`. Keep all consecutive notices, fields, and lines inside that same blockquote; separate windows when prose intervenes. Do not enclose System notices or UI terms in square brackets; the `System` heading and framed blockquote identify the panel. Do not label manuals, ordinary quotations, warnings printed in a manual, or other non-System material as `System`; use a normal blockquote or a specific heading instead. Do not wrap each complete notice in outer `**`; retain bold only for meaningful labels or emphasis inside the panel.
- Keep the final file English-only reading copy: no audit notes, Korean text, summaries, or model metadata.

### Tone and Style

- Write like a polished commercial webnovel: brisk, vivid, accessible, and easy to read aloud.
- Preserve the series’ contrast between danger and comedy. Let absurdity, bad timing, blunt reactions, and grim situations create dark humor without adding jokes absent from the Korean.
- Jin Taekyung’s narration is conversational, observant, self-mocking, and occasionally profane. It may be irreverent even when the situation is serious.
- Keep deadpan punchlines short and well-timed. Do not explain a joke after delivering it.
- Preserve the source's level of explicitness. A euphemism may remain euphemistic even when its meaning is sexual or crude; do not replace it with more graphic English merely for impact.
- Make dialogue spontaneous and character-specific. Preserve hierarchy and intimacy through word choice, address, rhythm, and restraint—not archaic wuxia English.
- Use strong profanity when the Korean is strong, but neither intensify nor sanitize it. Do not make ordinary lines uniformly vulgar. Profanity should reveal mood or relationship.
- Keep action and injury vivid but clear rather than purple. Do not make violence funny unless the source’s framing does.
- Avoid stiff literalism, translator-added melodrama, dated internet slang, and quippy superhero-style banter.
- On the second pass, correct awkward English collocations and word choices without changing meaning or voice. Prefer ordinary, spoken English over stiff Latinate or ceremonial wording when the scene is brisk or comic: “goose bumps” rather than “gooseflesh,” and “laid into them” rather than “launched into a solemn denunciation.” Read the prose aloud and replace any phrase that sounds like a formal essay, legal document, or literal dictionary gloss unless the source deliberately calls for that register.

## Footnotes

Use `[^1]` Markdown footnotes when a brief, factual, spoiler-free explanation materially helps an English reader understand:

- a Korean institution, living arrangement, food, holiday, myth, historical reference, or local custom;
- a Korean word, phrase, idiom, wordplay, or culturally specific image that cannot be conveyed fully by the best natural English analogy;
- a deliberately literal rendering whose cultural or linguistic force would otherwise be lost.

For example, render `고시원` as “goshiwon” when the setting or connotations matter, with a concise footnote explaining that it is a very small, inexpensive room-for-rent housing arrangement. Prefer the best natural English analogy in the prose. Use a literal translation plus a concise footnote when the Korean wording itself matters. Define a term at its first meaningful occurrence and do not repeat the note unnecessarily. Footnotes must be rare, useful, and non-spoiling; do not footnote ordinary vocabulary, fully preserved jokes, or uncertainty. Record consequential uncertainty in `docs/STATE.md`.

## Spoilers and Scope
